scenes.title: Meet Rohan and Friends
narration: Look at Rohan eating a juicy mango in the park.
Rohan is happy because Rohan loves mangoes.
Saying Rohan again sounds a bit silly, doesn't it?

scenes.title: What are Pronouns?
narration: A pronoun is a special word that replaces a noun.
Instead of Rohan, we can use the word He.
He is a pronoun, and it makes sentences flow better.

scenes.title: Seeing Pronouns in Action
narration: Priya has a red bag, so she carries it to school.
The dog is barking because it is hungry.
Rohan and Priya play, so they are best friends.

scenes.title: Quick Review
narration: Use He for boys, She for girls, and It for objects.
Use They when you are talking about more than one person.
Think about it: What pronoun would you use for your teacher?

scenes.title: Spotting Names Around You
narration: Look around your room in Delhi, what do you see?
Every person, place, and thing has a special name.
These naming words are called nouns.

scenes.title: Types of Nouns
narration: A noun can be a person like Aarav or a teacher.
It can be a place like a park or Mumbai.
It can even be a thing like a pen or a toy.

scenes.title: Noun Hunt Example
narration: Let us read this sentence together: Priya eats an apple.
Priya is the name of a girl, so it is a noun.
Apple is the name of a fruit, so it is also a noun.

scenes.title: Quick Recap
narration: Remember, nouns name people, places, and things.
They help us talk about everything in our world.
Can you find three nouns in your classroom right now?

scenes.title: Spotting Objects at Home
narration: Look around your room at home. Do you see an apple or a book?
Why do we say an apple but a book? Let us find out.
The secret hides in the starting sound of the word.

scenes.title: The Vowel Team
narration: Meet the vowels: A, E, I, O, and U.
If a word starts with a vowel sound, we use 'an'.
An orange and an umbrella start with these special sounds.

scenes.title: The Consonant Rule
narration: Other letters are consonants, like B, C, or D.
For words starting with a consonant, we use 'a'.
Like a ball or a car, we use 'a' here.

scenes.title: Quick Recap
narration: Use 'an' before vowels and 'a' before consonants.
Practice makes perfect! Can you say an egg or a cat?
Think about it: would you say a ice cream or an ice cream?

scenes.title: What Are You Doing?
narration: Look at Rohan playing in the park today.
He runs, he kicks, and he jumps.
Do you know what these special words are called?

scenes.title: Understanding Action Verbs
narration: These words are called verbs, or action words.
A verb tells us what a person or thing does.
Without verbs, our sentences would have no life.
Every sentence needs at least one verb to be complete.

scenes.title: Spotting Verbs at Home
narration: Let us look at Priya in her kitchen.
Priya eats a sweet mango.
She drinks a glass of cold milk.
She reads her storybook now.

scenes.title: Quick Review
narration: Verbs are words that show actions.
They tell us what someone is doing.
Think about it: what verbs can you find in your favorite book?

scenes.title: Spotting the Description
narration: Have you ever wondered why some stories feel so bright and exciting?
It is because we use special words to describe people, places, and things.
These helper words are called adjectives.

scenes.title: How Adjectives Work
narration: An adjective tells us more about a noun, like its size or color.
Instead of saying a dog, we say a fluffy dog.
The word fluffy is the adjective because it describes the dog.

scenes.title: A Trip to the Market
narration: Let us visit a busy market in Delhi to find adjectives.
Look, Rohan bought a juicy mango.
Juicy is the adjective describing the mango.
Next, he sees a tall man selling flowers.
Tall is the adjective describing the man.

scenes.title: Recap and Try It
narration: Adjectives help us paint pictures with our words.
They describe nouns by telling us about color, size, or shape.
Think about it: What three adjectives would you use to describe your best friend?

scenes.title: Spotting Action Words
narration: Look at Rohan playing in the park. What is he doing?
Rohan runs fast. Can you spot the action word?
Yes, runs is the action. But how does he run?

scenes.title: Introducing The Adverb
narration: We use a special word to tell us more about the action.
This helper word is called an adverb.
Adverbs describe how, when, or where an action happens.

scenes.title: Examples In Action
narration: Look, Meera eats her lunch slowly.
The word slowly tells us how she eats.
Now, the teacher speaks loudly in class.
Loudly is the adverb because it describes the speaking.

scenes.title: Recap And Practice
narration: Adverbs give us more details about actions.
Many adverbs end with the letters L Y.
Think about it: How would you describe how you walk today?

scenes.title: The Mystery of Many Items
narration: Have you noticed how we say apple for one, but apples for many?
When we have more than one thing, we usually add an s.
Let us see how to spot the difference in our bags.

scenes.title: Learning the Simple Rules
narration: Singular means there is only one of something.
Plural means there are two or more things together.
Adding an s makes most words turn from one to many.
Look at how a cup becomes cups.

scenes.title: Examples From Your Classroom
narration: Imagine you have one book on your desk.
Now, your friend brings three more books.
We write it as book plus s equals books.
See how easy it is to change the word?

scenes.title: Quick Recap and Challenge
narration: Singular is one, and plural is many things.
Most times, we just add an s at the end.
Think about it: how would you write the plural of pen?

scenes.title: Meet the Sentence Parts
narration: Have you ever wondered how we build a full sentence when we speak?
Every sentence has two main parts: a subject and a predicate.
Let us learn how these two pieces work together to share ideas.

scenes.title: The Subject and Predicate
narration: The subject tells us who or what the sentence is about.
The predicate tells us what the subject is doing or being.
Together, they make a complete thought that everyone can understand.

scenes.title: See It in Action
narration: Look at this sentence: Rohan eats a mango.
Rohan is the subject because he is the person doing the action.
Eats a mango is the predicate because it tells us his action.

scenes.title: Quick Recap
narration: Remember, the subject is the who, and the predicate is the action.
Both parts are needed to make a perfect sentence every time.
Think about it: Can you name the subject in your own sentence?

scenes.title: The Magic Glue
narration: Have you ever wanted to join two short sentences into one big, fun sentence?
We use special connecting words called conjunctions to link our thoughts together.
Let's see how words like and, but, and or help us speak better.

scenes.title: Using And, But, Or
narration: We use and to add things together, like saying I like cricket and football.
We use but to show a difference, like saying it is sunny but very cold.
We use or to show a choice, like asking do you want milk or tea?

scenes.title: Let Us Practice
narration: Look at Rohan. He likes mangoes. He likes bananas too.
We can combine them to say Rohan likes mangoes and bananas.
Now, imagine it is raining. We want to go to the park.
We say it is raining, but we want to go to the park.

scenes.title: Quick Recap
narration: Conjunctions like and, but, and or are tools to make longer, smoother sentences.
Practice using these words when you write your next school story.
Think about it: Can you write one sentence about your favorite meal using the word and?

scenes.title: Finding Things Around Us
narration: Have you ever lost your favorite toy and had to hunt for it?
Today we will learn how to tell exactly where things are hiding.
These helper words are called prepositions.

scenes.title: Understanding Preposition Positions
narration: A preposition shows the position of a noun.
Use the word in when something is inside a space.
Use on when it is sitting right on top.
Use under if it is hidden below something else.

scenes.title: A Cricket Match Example
narration: Rohan is playing cricket in his garden.
The cricket ball is in the red bag.
Now, the ball is on the wooden bench.
Oh no, the ball is under the mango tree!

scenes.title: Recap and Practice
narration: Prepositions like in, on, and under tell us where things are.
They help us describe the world clearly.
Think about it: Where is your school bag right now?

scenes.title: What Will You Do?
narration: Look at your calendar, what will you do tomorrow?
We use special words to talk about things that have not happened yet.
Let us learn how to use will to talk about the future.

scenes.title: Using The Word Will
narration: To talk about the future, we just add the word will.
We put will before the action word, like this.
So, instead of I run, we say I will run.
It works the same for he, she, they, or Rohan.

scenes.title: An Example At School
narration: Imagine Rohan is at his desk in class.
Rohan has a book in his hand today.
Tomorrow, Rohan will read a new story.
See how we added will before the word read?

scenes.title: Time To Recap
narration: Use will to talk about things happening later.
Place will right before the action word.
Think about it: what will you eat for dinner tonight?

scenes.title: What do you do daily?
narration: Do you brush your teeth every single morning?
We use the simple present tense to talk about things we do every day.
Let us learn how to speak about our routines correctly.

scenes.title: Using the right verbs
narration: For I, you, we, and they, just use the verb word.
Example: I eat a tasty dosa for breakfast.
When we say he, she, or it, we add an s to the verb.
Example: She eats a healthy apple every morning.

scenes.title: A trip to the park
narration: Look at Rohan playing in the park.
Rohan plays with his red ball.
His friends run fast on the grass.

scenes.title: Quick recap and challenge
narration: Remember, add s for he, she, and it.
Keep verbs plain for I, you, we, and they.
Think about it: what is one thing your best friend does every day?

scenes.title: The Big Question
narration: Look at Rohan playing in the park.
Have you ever wondered how to describe things happening right this second?
Today we learn how to say what is happening now.

scenes.title: The Secret Formula
narration: To show action now, use a helping verb like am, is, or are.
Then, take your action word and add i-n-g to the end.
Like jump becomes jumping, or play becomes playing.

scenes.title: Using It Together
narration: If I am alone, I say I am reading a book.
If Meera is near, we say she is eating a mango.
When they are in a group, we say they are running fast.

scenes.title: Quick Recap Time
narration: Remember, use am, is, or are plus an action word with i-n-g.
This tells us exactly what is happening at this very moment.
Think about it: what are your friends doing in the classroom right now?

scenes.title: What Happened Yesterday?
narration: Rohan played cricket in the park yesterday.
Do you know how to talk about things that are already done?
We use the simple past tense for completed actions.

scenes.title: Adding ED to Verbs
narration: Most verbs change by adding ed at the end.
Walk becomes walked, like Meera walked to school.
Jump becomes jumped, like the cat jumped high.

scenes.title: Practicing With Sentences
narration: Let us try a sentence with play.
I play with my toys becomes I played with my toys.
The action is finished, so we use played.

scenes.title: Quick Review
narration: Remember, add ed to show the past.
It tells us the action happened before now.
Think about it: what game did you play yesterday?

scenes.title: Spot the Hidden Twins
narration: Look at this happy boy named Rohan playing in the park.
Rohan says he is glad to be here today.
Did you know glad means the exact same thing as happy?

scenes.title: Learning About Synonyms
narration: Words that have the same meaning are called synonyms.
Synonyms are like different names for the same toy.
Using them makes our stories much more exciting to read.

scenes.title: Examples in Our Day
narration: If a dosa is very big, you can say it is large.
If your bag is fast, you can call it quick.
If a kitten is tiny, you can say it is small.

scenes.title: Quick Recap
narration: Synonyms are different words that share the same meaning.
They help us describe things in brand new ways.
Think about it: Can you find a synonym for the word cold?

scenes.title: The Curious Detective
narration: Have you ever wondered how to find out something new?
We use special words to ask questions about our world.
Let's discover the magic of words like Who, What, and Where.

scenes.title: Three Important Words
narration: We use Who to ask about a person.
We use What to ask about a thing or action.
We use Where to ask about a place.

scenes.title: A Day With Rohan
narration: Who is eating a mango? It is Rohan.
What is Rohan holding? A tasty yellow mango.
Where is Rohan sitting? Under a tree in the park.

scenes.title: Quick Recap
narration: Who asks for people, What for things, and Where for places.
Using these words helps you become a great detective.
Think about it: What question would you ask your best friend today?

scenes.title: The Messy Story
narration: Have you ever read a story with no dots or commas?
It looks like a big jumble of words, doesn't it?
Today, let's learn how punctuation fixes our sentences.

scenes.title: Meet The Punctuators
narration: A full stop ends a sentence like a gentle break.
A comma lets you take a tiny breath while reading.
A question mark asks something, like where are you going?
An exclamation mark shows strong feelings like excitement!

scenes.title: Rahul at the Market
narration: Rahul went to the market to buy apples bananas and milk.
Without commas, it is hard to tell what he bought.
Now we add them: Rahul bought apples, bananas, and milk.
See how the commas separate the items clearly?

scenes.title: Wrap Up and Review
narration: Full stops stop, commas pause, and question marks ask.
Exclamation marks show big feelings, like Yay or Oh!
Think about it: how would your sentence change if you forgot the period?

scenes.title: Spotting the Hidden Rules
narration: Have you noticed some letters in books are taller than others?
These big letters are called capital letters.
Do you know when we must use them?

scenes.title: Starting Every Sentence Right
narration: Every new sentence must begin with a capital letter.
Look at this: The cat sits.
The T is big, just like a starter should be.

scenes.title: Names Need Big Letters Too
narration: Names of people always get a capital letter at the start.
If you write about Rohan or Priya, use a capital letter.
Even special places like Delhi need one too.
It shows they are very important words.

scenes.title: Time to Remember
narration: Always use capitals for the start of sentences and names.
They help our writing look neat and easy to read.
Can you find a name in your book that needs a capital letter?

scenes.title: What Are Prefixes
narration: Have you ever seen the word happy turn into unhappy?
Adding letters to the front changes a word's meaning.
These helper letters are called prefixes.

scenes.title: How Prefixes Work
narration: A prefix is a little piece added to the start.
It transforms the base word into something new.
It is like putting a hat on a word.

scenes.title: Examples In Action
narration: Take the word tie and add un- to make untie.
Take the word view and add re- to make review.
Take the word happy and add un- to make unhappy.

scenes.title: Recap And Challenge
narration: Prefixes go at the front to change meaning.
They help us build many more words easily.
Think about it, what happens if you add un- to kind?

scenes.title: What Are Opposites
narration: Look at your tall school building and the tiny ants on the ground.
Tall and tiny are opposites, which we call antonyms.
Antonyms are words that have the opposite meaning.

scenes.title: Spotting Simple Antonyms
narration: Let us look at some pairs together.
Hot tea in your cup and cold ice cream.
A fast car and a slow turtle.
The sun is bright but the moon is dark.

scenes.title: Using Antonyms Correctly
narration: Rohan is happy because he won a game.
When he loses, he feels sad.
Happy and sad are perfect antonyms.
We use these to describe how we feel.

scenes.title: Quick Review
narration: Antonyms are just opposite words.
They help make our sentences more interesting.
Can you think of the antonym for big?

scenes.title: The Mystery Of Similar Sounds
narration: Have you ever heard two words that sound exactly the same but mean different things?
These special words are called homophones.
Let us discover how to tell them apart at home.

scenes.title: Learning The Concept
narration: Homophones sound the same, like two friends calling out to you.
But they have different spellings and different meanings.
Thinking about the meaning helps us pick the right one.

scenes.title: Real Life Examples
narration: Take the word sun, which shines brightly in the sky.
Now take the word son, which means a boy child.
See how they sound the same but mean something totally different?
Another pair is blue, the color, and blew, like the wind.

scenes.title: Recap And Practice
narration: Homophones sound alike but have different spellings.
Always check the meaning before you write them down.
Can you think of any other homophones you use at school?

scenes.title: Spotting Two Little Words
narration: Have you ever noticed that some big words are just two small words joined together?
Look at the word housefly. It is made of house and fly.
We call these special words compound words.

scenes.title: How They Work
narration: Think of it like building with blocks.
You take one word and push it right next to another.
When they touch, they become one brand new word.
The new word has a new meaning too.

scenes.title: Let Us Build Some
narration: Let us take the word rain and add the word bow.
Together, they make the word rainbow.
How about foot plus ball?
That makes football, a game we love to play.

scenes.title: Recap and Challenge
narration: Compound words are just two words joined to make one new word.
They are easy to spot once you know the trick.
Think about it, can you find a compound word in your own lunchbox today?

scenes.title: The Mystery of Word Endings
narration: Have you ever noticed how some words change when we add a little piece to the end?
Meet the suffix, a tiny group of letters that hops onto the end of a word.
Adding a suffix creates a brand new word with a special meaning.

scenes.title: Learning the Suffix Rules
narration: First is -ing, which shows an action is happening right now, like playing in the park.
Then we have -ed, which tells us something already finished yesterday, like walked.
And -er helps us compare, like saying a cheetah is faster than a rabbit.

scenes.title: Suffixes in Action
narration: Look at the word jump. Add -ing and it becomes jumping, like you on a trampoline.
Now take the word help. Add -ed to show you helped your friend share their lunch.
Take the word tall. Add -er to say your brother is taller than you.

scenes.title: Recap and Challenge
narration: Suffixes go at the end of words to help us explain time and comparisons clearly.
Remember, just add them to the end of a base word to create something new.
Think about it: can you find a word with a suffix in your favorite storybook today?

scenes.title: The Mystery Word
narration: Have you ever found a word in a book you did not know?
Do not worry, you can be a word detective right now!
We use clues in sentences to find the meaning.

scenes.title: Finding Your Clues
narration: Look at the words right before your mystery word.
Check the words that come after it too.
These surrounding words are called context.

scenes.title: A Story Example
narration: Rahul felt famished because he skipped lunch today.
Famished is a tricky word, but look at the clues.
He skipped lunch, so he must be very hungry.
Now we know famished means super hungry!

scenes.title: Become A Pro
narration: Remember, check the clues around your mystery word.
Use the story to help you guess the meaning.
Think about it: What clues help you understand a word you just read?

scenes.title: Spotting Secret Patterns
narration: Have you noticed how some words look like twins?
Look at the words cat, hat, and mat.
They all end with the same sound, at.

scenes.title: Learning Word Families
narration: Words that share a sound belong to a word family.
Just change the first letter to make a new friend.
The ending stays the same, like a family name.

scenes.title: Building The Ig Family
narration: Let us build words with the ig family.
Add a p to get pig.
Add a w to get wig.
Add a d to get dig.

scenes.title: Review And Practice
narration: Word families make reading and writing so much faster.
Remember to look for the pattern at the end.
Can you think of three words that end in an?

scenes.title: The Mystery of Words
narration: Have you ever found a word in a book you did not know?
You can use a dictionary to find the meaning of any word.
But how do we find them when there are thousands of words inside?

scenes.title: The Alphabet Secret
narration: Dictionaries are organized by the alphabet, just like a list of names.
Words starting with A come first, then B, and all the way to Z.
If two words start with the same letter, look at the second letter.
In cat and cup, A comes before U, so cat comes first.

scenes.title: Let's Find 'Mango'
narration: Let us find the word mango in our dictionary.
First, we flip the pages to the M section.
Next, we look for words starting with ma.
Finally, we spot mango right there on the page.

scenes.title: Recap and Practice
narration: Remember, dictionaries follow the alphabet to keep words in order.
Always look at the first letter, then the second to find your word.
Think about it: which word comes first in a dictionary, apple or ant?

scenes.title: What Are Fables
narration: Have you ever heard a story where animals talk and teach a lesson?
These short stories are called fables, and they are very fun to read.
Every fable has a special message called a moral at the end.

scenes.title: How Fables Work
narration: Fables usually have only two or three characters.
The characters often act like humans to show us right from wrong.
They face a problem, try to solve it, and learn a big lesson.

scenes.title: The Tortoise and the Hare
narration: Think of the story where the fast Hare races the slow Tortoise.
The Hare is lazy, but the Tortoise keeps going without stopping.
The Tortoise wins because he works hard and never gives up.

scenes.title: Recap and Think
narration: Fables use animals to teach us important life lessons.
Look for the moral at the end of every fable you read.
Think about it: What is your favorite animal, and what lesson could it teach?

scenes.title: The Magic of Reading
narration: Do you ever wonder how paper pages turn into exciting adventures?
Reading is like having a secret key to open any door.
Let us learn how to read stories like a true detective.

scenes.title: Finding the Clues
narration: Every good story has characters, like Aarav or a brave cat.
The setting tells us where the story happens, maybe in a park.
The plot is just the sequence of events that take place.

scenes.title: A Story Example
narration: Imagine Meena finds a shiny golden key in her garden.
She uses the key to open an old wooden box.
Inside, she finds a map to a hidden treasure chest.

scenes.title: Recap and Explore
narration: Remember, always look for characters, the setting, and the plot.
Reading is the best way to travel without leaving your room.
Think about it: who is your favorite character in any story?

scenes.title: What Makes a Poem?
narration: Have you ever noticed how some stories sound like a catchy song?
Poems are special because they use rhythm and rhyming words.
Let us see why words like cat and mat belong together.

scenes.title: Understanding Rhyme
narration: A rhyme happens when two words end with the same sound.
Like the word bat and the word hat.
The ending at sounds exactly the same in both.

scenes.title: Let's Read a Poem
narration: Rohan ate a sweet red apple in the park.
Then he heard a dog give a loud bark.
Apple and bark do not rhyme, but park and bark do!
Park and bark both end with the ark sound.

scenes.title: Recap and Practice
narration: Remember, poems use rhyming words to create a fun beat.
Listen for the same ending sounds when you read aloud.
Can you find a word that rhymes with sun for your next poem?

scenes.title: Finding the Hook
narration: Have you ever wondered how to find facts in your favorite book?
Reading informational passages helps us learn about our world.
Let's explore how to read like a detective today.

scenes.title: The Big Ideas
narration: First, look for the main topic in the title.
Next, scan for bold words that give clues.
Read the first sentence to find the main idea.
Always check pictures for more information.

scenes.title: A Tiger Example
narration: Look at a passage about the Bengal Tiger.
The title says: The Bengal Tiger's Home.
We see a bold word: Habitat.
It means the place where tigers live.
The picture shows them in a forest.

scenes.title: Summing Up
narration: Remember to use titles, bold words, and pictures.
These help you understand new facts quickly.
Think about it: what new fact will you learn today?

scenes.title: The Big Secret
narration: Have you ever wondered what a story is really about?
We look for the main idea to find the story's heart.
It is the most important message the author shares.

scenes.title: How to Find It
narration: First, read the whole story carefully.
Next, look for words that repeat often.
Finally, ask yourself what the story is teaching.

scenes.title: A Trip to Delhi
narration: Riya visited the Red Fort and saw the India Gate.
She ate yummy jalebis and saw the busy markets.
The main idea is that Riya had a fun day in Delhi.

scenes.title: Wrap Up
narration: Remember, the main idea is the big point, not just little details.
You are now ready to be a reading detective.
What is the main idea of your favorite book?

scenes.title: The Big Mystery Idea
narration: Have you ever wondered why some stories have so many extra sentences?
A main idea is like the trunk of a big mango tree.
The supporting details are like the branches holding the fruit.

scenes.title: How Details Help Us
narration: Supporting details give us more information about the main point.
They answer questions like who, what, where, or why.
Without them, a story would be very short and boring.

scenes.title: A Day at the Market
narration: Main idea: Rohan went to the busy Delhi market today.
Detail one: He bought three juicy red apples.
Detail two: He saw a colorful kite flying high.
Detail three: The shopkeeper gave him a friendly smile.

scenes.title: Quick Review Time
narration: Remember, the main idea is the big topic.
Supporting details are the clues that explain it better.
Think about it: Can you find two details in your favorite book today?

scenes.title: Finding The Story Characters
narration: Have you ever wondered who the people in your favorite stories are?
A character is a person, animal, or creature in a story.
They think, feel, and do things just like you do!

scenes.title: Looking For Clues
narration: To find a character, look for their name in the book.
Look for words that tell us what they do, like runs or jumps.
Notice how they speak in the story using quotation marks.

scenes.title: Meet Little Rohan
narration: Let us look at a story about Rohan who loves to draw.
Rohan picks up his blue pencil and smiles big.
Rohan says, I am drawing a big sun today.
We know Rohan is the character because he acts and speaks.

scenes.title: Recap And Think
narration: Characters can be people, animals, or even robots.
Find them by watching what they do and say.
Think about it: who is your favorite character and why?

scenes.title: A Day in Order
narration: Have you ever wondered why stories have a beginning, middle, and end?
Think about your morning before you come to school.
You wake up, eat breakfast, and pack your bag.

scenes.title: What is Sequence?
narration: Sequence is just a fancy word for putting things in the right order.
When reading, we look for clues like first, then, and finally.
If we mix the order up, the story sounds silly!

scenes.title: Making Aloo Paratha
narration: Let us see how Rohan makes a yummy aloo paratha.
First, he mashes the boiled potatoes with spices.
Next, he stuffs the dough and rolls it flat.
Finally, he cooks it on the hot tawa until golden.

scenes.title: Recap and Think
narration: Remember, stories happen in a specific order to make sense.
Always look for those special sequence words while you read.
Think about it: What would happen if we ate dinner before breakfast?

scenes.title: What are Inferences
narration: Have you ever looked at a friend and known they were happy without them saying a word?
That is called an inference, and we use it to understand stories better!
An inference is like being a detective using clues to find the hidden meaning.

scenes.title: Finding Hidden Clues
narration: Authors do not always tell us everything directly in the text.
We look at the words on the page and add what we already know.
This combination helps us guess what is happening in the story.

scenes.title: Example in Action
narration: Imagine Rohan is wearing a raincoat and holding a wet umbrella.
The text says he is dripping wet and walking through puddles.
We know it is raining outside, even if the story never says it!

scenes.title: Recap and Challenge
narration: Remember, use text clues and what you know to make a smart guess.
Inferences turn reading into an exciting mystery for you to solve.
Think about it: If a character is shivering, what can you guess about the weather?

scenes.title: The Mystery Word Challenge
narration: Have you ever read a book and found a word you did not know?
Don't worry, because you can be a word detective!
Today we will learn how to guess meanings using clues around the word.

scenes.title: Looking for Context Clues
narration: Context clues are the other words in the sentence that give us hints.
First, look at the words right before and after the new word.
Think about what is happening in the story to help you guess.
The sentence often explains the meaning if you read it carefully.

scenes.title: Solving a Word Puzzle
narration: Let us try this: Rohan felt exhausted after playing cricket for three hours.
What does exhausted mean? Look at the clue: he played for three hours.
If you play sports for a long time, you feel very tired.
So, exhausted means very, very tired!

scenes.title: Recap and Try It
narration: Remember, be a detective and look for clues in the sentence.
Check if your guess makes sense in the story.
Can you find a new word today and guess its meaning?

scenes.title: The Big Hook
narration: Have you ever wanted to tell a story about your favorite park or a trip to Delhi?
Writing a paragraph is like building a house for your ideas.
Do you know what makes a perfect paragraph?

scenes.title: The Three Main Parts
narration: First, the topic sentence tells everyone exactly what you are writing about.
Next, you add supporting sentences that give juicy details.
Lastly, the closing sentence wraps everything up nicely.

scenes.title: Let's Write Together
narration: Let us write about a mango. Start with: The mango is a delicious fruit.
Next, add a detail: It is bright yellow and very sweet.
Finish it with: I love eating mangoes in summer.

scenes.title: Recap and Try
narration: Remember, a paragraph needs a beginning, middle details, and a clear end.
Keep your sentences focused on one single idea.
Think about it: What is one thing you want to write a paragraph about today?

scenes.title: The Big Story Idea
narration: Have you ever imagined a dragon living in a school canteen in Delhi?
Stories are just your imagination written down on paper.
Every great story needs a hero and something exciting to happen.

scenes.title: Building Your Story Map
narration: First, introduce your hero in the beginning.
Next, show a problem they need to solve.
Finally, explain how they fix it to finish the story.

scenes.title: Writing About Ravi
narration: Let us write about Ravi, a boy who lost his cricket ball.
Ravi looks for his ball under a big mango tree.
Suddenly, he finds it inside a friendly neighbor's garden.

scenes.title: Reviewing Your Work
narration: Remember to use capital letters and full stops in every sentence.
Always read your story aloud to hear if it sounds fun.
Think about it: If you were a superhero, what would your first mission be?

scenes.title: The Magic of Letters
narration: Have you ever received a surprise letter in the post from a friend?
Writing a letter is a special way to share news with someone far away.
Let's learn how to write a friendly informal letter today!

scenes.title: Parts of a Letter
narration: First, write your address and the date at the top right corner.
Next, start with a warm greeting like Dear Rohan.
Then, write the main message in a few simple sentences.
Finally, add a closing like Your friend, followed by your name.

scenes.title: Writing to Priya
narration: Let's write to our friend Priya about our new pet kitten.
Start with Dear Priya, and say how are you.
I have a tiny kitten named Mittu, she is very soft.
End with, See you soon, Love, Rahul.

scenes.title: Recap and Think
narration: Remember to include the date, greeting, your message, and a closing.
Keep your words friendly, just like how you talk to friends.
Think about it: who would you like to send your first letter to?

scenes.title: What is a diary?
narration: Have you ever wanted to keep your own secret book?
A diary is a special place to write about your day.
It is like telling a story to yourself.

scenes.title: How to start writing
narration: Always start by writing today's date at the top.
Next, say hello to your diary, like Dear Diary.
Use the word I when you talk about yourself.
Always remember to use past tense for things finished.

scenes.title: Let's write an entry
narration: Imagine you visited the zoo with Rohan today.
Write, I saw a tall giraffe at the zoo.
Then write, I ate a yummy mango ice cream.
End with, I had a very fun day.

scenes.title: Recap and Practice
narration: Remember, date first, greeting next, and talk about you.
Keep your diary safe and write in it every day.
What is one fun thing you will write about tonight?

scenes.title: Look at the Picture
narration: Have you ever looked at a picture and wondered what is happening inside it?
Pictures are like frozen stories waiting for you to tell them.
Today we will learn how to write about a picture in three easy steps.

scenes.title: The Three Magic Steps
narration: First, list what you see, like people, animals, or objects.
Next, describe what is happening using action words.
Finally, add feelings to tell us if the scene is happy or calm.

scenes.title: Writing About a Park
narration: Imagine a picture of Rohan playing in a sunny park.
Step one: I see Rohan, a ball, and a big green tree.
Step two: Rohan is kicking the ball on the grass.
Step three: Rohan has a big smile because he is happy.

scenes.title: Recap and Challenge
narration: Remember to list things, describe actions, and share feelings.
Your sentences will make the picture come alive for the reader.
Think about it: What story would you write about a picture of a rainy day?

scenes.title: The Magic of Describing
narration: Have you ever told a friend about a yummy treat you ate?
Instead of saying it was good, can you make them taste it?
Descriptive writing helps you paint a picture in the reader's mind.

scenes.title: Using Your Five Senses
narration: First, use your senses to find special details.
Does the object look bright, feel soft, or smell sweet?
These details make your sentences come alive for everyone.

scenes.title: Example: Describing a Mango
narration: Let us describe a ripe, juicy mango from the market.
Instead of saying 'it is yellow', say 'the mango is bright golden'.
Add a feeling: 'It feels smooth and heavy in my hand.'
Finish with taste: 'The fruit is sweet like honey.'

scenes.title: Recap and Try It
narration: Remember to use your five senses to add color to your writing.
Pick better words to show, not just tell, what you see.
Think about it: How would you describe your favorite school bag?

scenes.title: The Big Mystery
narration: Have you ever told a friend about a story you read?
You do not tell them every single word, right?
Summarizing is picking only the most important parts.

scenes.title: Finding the Gold
narration: First, read your passage carefully from start to finish.
Then, ask yourself: Who is this story about?
Next, ask: What is the main thing that happened?
Ignore the small details that do not change the plot.

scenes.title: A Story Example
narration: Rohan went to the park and ate a red apple.
He played cricket with friends until the sun set.
A short summary is: Rohan played cricket at the park.
See? We kept the hero and the main action.

scenes.title: Wrap It Up
narration: Remember, a summary is short and tells the main idea.
Always use your own words to describe the story.
Can you summarize your favorite book in just three sentences?

scenes.title: The Hook
narration: Have you ever shared a funny story about your day at school?
Do you want to know how to make your tales super exciting?
Let us learn the secrets to being a great storyteller today!

scenes.title: The Idea
narration: First, start with a clear beginning to introduce your characters.
Next, add a middle part where something interesting or tricky happens.
Finally, give your story a happy or clever ending.
Use feeling words to help your friends picture the scene.

scenes.title: The Example
narration: Imagine Rohan finds a shiny gold coin at the park.
Suddenly, a friendly squirrel tries to take his treasure!
Rohan trades a nut for the coin and smiles big.
See how using 'shiny', 'friendly', and 'big' makes it better?

scenes.title: The Recap
narration: Remember to have a clear beginning, middle, and end.
Use exciting words to bring your story to life.
Think about it: what is one exciting story you can tell your family tonight?

scenes.title: The Magic of Talking
narration: Have you ever wondered how to make your friend feel happy while you talk?
A conversation is like a game of catch with words.
Do you listen as much as you speak?

scenes.title: Taking Turns to Speak
narration: First, wait for your friend to finish their sentence completely.
Look at them kindly so they know you are listening.
When it is your turn, use a clear voice to share your thoughts.
Avoid interrupting, just like waiting for your turn on the swing.

scenes.title: A Chat at School
narration: Imagine Rohan tells you, I loved the history lesson today.
You should reply, That is great, what was your favorite part?
Rohan says, I liked learning about the Taj Mahal.
You respond, Me too, the white marble is beautiful!

scenes.title: Remembering Your Skills
narration: Remember to listen carefully, take turns, and ask good questions.
Conversations are much better when everyone feels heard.
Think about it: Who will you have a kind conversation with today?

scenes.title: The Magic of Ideas
narration: Do you ever look at a blank page and wonder what to write?
Writing is like painting a picture in your reader's mind.
Let's learn how to turn your thoughts into an amazing story.

scenes.title: Building Your Story World
narration: First, pick a hero, like Ayesha who loves to explore.
Next, decide where she goes, like a bustling Delhi market.
Then, give her a problem to solve, like finding a lost key.
Finally, show how she solves it using her brave heart.

scenes.title: A Story in Action
narration: Ayesha walked through the busy market smelling fresh spicy samosas.
She looked for her key under a bright red stall.
Suddenly, a friendly cat tapped her shiny silver key.
Ayesha smiled because her mystery was solved at last.

scenes.title: Time to Write
narration: Remember to use your five senses to make stories feel real.
Always check your sentences start with capitals and end with stops.
Now, what is one exciting adventure you want to write about?

scenes.title: Why Ask Questions
narration: Have you ever wondered why the sky is blue or how a bird flies?
Asking questions is the best way to learn new things every single day.
Let's learn how to ask clear questions to get the best answers.

scenes.title: The Question Starters
narration: Use special words like Who, What, Where, When, Why, and How.
Who asks about a person, like Who is your best friend?
What asks about a thing, like What is for lunch today?
Where asks for a place, like Where is my red school bag?

scenes.title: Practice With Rahul
narration: Rahul wants to know about a trip to the Taj Mahal.
He asks, When can we go to Agra to see it?
He also asks, How do we get there by train?
By using these words, Rahul gets all the information he needs.

scenes.title: Time To Practice
narration: Remember to use who, what, where, when, why, or how.
Listen carefully to the answer so you can learn even more.
Think about it: what is one question you want to ask your teacher today?

scenes.title: The Hook
narration: Have you ever told a friend about your amazing day at the park?
Sometimes it is hard to explain exactly what happened, right?
Today, we will learn how to describe events so others can picture them!

scenes.title: The Three Steps
narration: First, start by saying when and where the event happened.
Next, use action words to tell us what happened in order.
Finally, add a feeling word to describe how it made you feel.

scenes.title: A Day at the Fair
narration: Yesterday, I went to the village fair in Jaipur.
I bought a balloon and rode the spinning merry-go-round.
I felt so excited because the music was very loud!

scenes.title: Recap and Think
narration: Remember to share the when, the what, and your feelings.
Using these steps makes your stories fun to hear!
Think about it: What is one fun thing you did this weekend?

scenes.title: The Mystery of Lost Directions
narration: Have you ever tried to explain a game to a friend but they got confused?
Giving good instructions is like following a map to find hidden treasure.
Today, we will learn how to speak so everyone understands us perfectly.

scenes.title: Three Steps to Success
narration: First, use short and simple sentences so your friend can follow along.
Second, speak in the right order like steps in a recipe.
Third, use polite words like please when you ask for help.
Always check if your listener understands by asking them a quick question.

scenes.title: Making a Jam Sandwich
narration: Let us tell Rahul how to make a yummy jam sandwich.
First, please put two slices of bread on a clean plate.
Next, spread the sweet jam on one slice using a knife.
Finally, put the other slice on top and enjoy your snack.

scenes.title: Recap and Try It
narration: Remember to use simple steps and always be polite when you talk.
Clear instructions help everyone work together happily at school and home.
Think about it: what instructions would you give to teach someone a game?

scenes.title: Why Listen Carefully?
narration: Have you ever missed a cool instruction because you were busy playing?
Listening is more than just hearing sounds around you.
It is like catching a ball with your ears instead of your hands.

scenes.title: The Three Steps
narration: First, look at the person who is speaking to you.
Second, stay quiet so you can hear every important word.
Third, think about what they mean before you answer.

scenes.title: An Example at School
narration: Imagine your teacher says, Bring your notebook to my desk.
If you are listening, you hear three things: notebook, desk, and bring.
Instead of running to the playground, you walk to the teacher.

scenes.title: Recap and Try It
narration: Remember: Look, stay quiet, and think to be a super listener.
Listening helps you learn faster and make fewer mistakes.
Think about it: What is one thing you will listen for today?

scenes.title: The Magic of Pretend
narration: Have you ever pretended to be a shopkeeper or a doctor?
Role-play is acting out a situation to learn how we talk to others.
It helps us practice using kind and clear words.

scenes.title: Steps to Great Acting
narration: First, choose your character and where the story happens.
Next, think about what your character wants to say.
Then, listen carefully to your partner before you speak.

scenes.title: A Day at the Market
narration: Imagine Rohan is buying apples from a fruit seller.
Rohan says, Hello, may I please buy two apples?
The seller says, Yes, that will be ten rupees.
Rohan replies, Thank you, have a nice day!

scenes.title: Time to Wrap Up
narration: Role-playing helps us speak clearly and listen with respect.
Always use polite words like please, thank you, and excuse me.
Think about it: who would you like to be in a role-play today?
